summary.one_line: SRIT India is a Bengaluru government IT system integrator. About 89% of its revenue comes from tenders, it relies heavily on subcontractors, and its receivables are swelling. The Rs.218.4 cr all-fresh issue mostly funds working capital and unidentified acquisitions. Profit growth is real, but cash generation, concentration and the business model make this one to avoid.
bull_points: Revenue from operations grew from Rs.2,710.88 mn in FY24 to Rs.4,499.99 mn in FY26 (28.84% CAGR), and PAT from Rs.290.76 mn to Rs.432.89 mn (S1)
The order book was Rs.12,047.17 mn at 30 June 2026, roughly 2.7x FY26 revenue, spread over 102 ongoing orders (S1)
The issue is 100% fresh with no offer for sale, so every rupee raised goes to the company (S1, S4)

It has a 26-year delivery record, CMMI Level 5 and SSE-CMM appraisals, and has executed large state projects such as a Rs.5,557.80 mn state-wide fibre network and a Rs.2,508.19 mn 4G ATM-connectivity migration for a public sector bank (S1)
The client repeat rate rose from 61.33% in FY24 to 73.85% in FY26 (S1)
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative Rs.121.01 mn in FY26 even though restated PAT was Rs.432.89 mn. Trade receivables plus contract assets reached Rs.3,855.53 mn, or 63.27% of total assets (S1)
Government entities provided 89.41% of FY26 revenue and the top 10 customers 89.36%. Work is won by tender, with a bid win ratio of 13.95% in FY26 (S1)

Subcontracting and technical fees were 78.92% of total expenses in FY26, and 59% of revenue came from projects executed through third-party subcontractors. SRIT is mostly an integrator and project manager, not an IP owner (S1)
The order book is shrinking: Rs.14,769.56 mn (FY24) to Rs.12,160.55 mn (FY25) to Rs.11,828.24 mn (FY26). FY26 new awards were Rs.3,263.22 mn against Rs.4,499.99 mn of revenue billed (S1)
Up to 35% of gross proceeds goes to unidentified acquisitions plus general corporate purposes. No target has been identified and no definitive agreement signed (S1)
watch_points: Whether FY27 operating cash flow turns positive, and whether contract assets (Rs.1,538.01 mn in FY26, up from Rs.964.32 mn) get billed and collected (S1)
Final-day QIB and NII subscription (day-1 data was not meaningful when this was written) and the anchor 30-day and 90-day lock-in expiries (S5, S8)
Use of the unallocated acquisition money: any deal should be read against the RHP's promise that no target will come from the promoter group or related parties (S1)
Resolution of the ASB arbitration, the Galmax claim of about Rs.25.16 mn, and total contingent liabilities of about Rs.634 mn at FY26 (S1, S6)

reasoning: The business earns accounting profit but not cash. FY26 PAT was Rs.432.89 mn, yet operating cash flow was negative Rs.121.01 mn. Receivables plus unbilled contract assets are Rs.3,855.53 mn, about 313 days of FY26 revenue by my calculation, and Rs.136 mn of receivables are more than three years old. Rs.1,240 mn of the issue (about 57% of the gross issue) goes to working capital, which confirms that growth consumes cash rather than produces it (S1)

There is no real moat. SRIT wins government tenders mostly on price and pre-qualification, then subcontracts most of the delivery: subcontracting was 78.92% of total expenses. Its listed peers include RailTel, which is also one of its top ten customers. Certifications and track record are the industry's entry ticket, not a barrier (S1)

Revenue quality is fragile. 89.41% comes from government, the top 3 customers are 57.93%, and five states give about 76% of revenue. The order book has fallen two years running, and FY26 awards (Rs.3,263.22 mn) did not replace what was billed. Healthcare, the vertical where most of the product capex goes, fell from Rs.596.77 mn to Rs.330.51 mn of revenue (S1)

Much of the issue is a blank cheque. Apart from Rs.128.57 mn of product capex and the working capital, the balance (capped at 35% of gross proceeds) goes to acquisitions with no identified target plus general corporate purposes. The capex estimates rely on vendor quotations with no orders placed, and the proceeds deployment has not been appraised by any bank or financial institution (S1)

Capital history favours insiders. In September 2024 the company spent Rs.207.84 mn buying back shares from the three promoters while borrowing. Promoter loans were converted to equity at Rs.70 in April 2025, and pre-IPO placements were done at Rs.95 in August to November 2025, against a Rs.130 cap price. Auditors' emphasis-of-matter notes flag MSME non-disclosure, CSR non-provision and struck-off subsidiaries. None of this is fraud, but it is weak governance for a first-time listing (S1)

blocks.text: SRIT India is a Bengaluru-headquartered IT/ITeS company incorporated in September 1999. It designs, implements and operates digital platforms, custom applications and system-integration projects, overwhelmingly for central and state government bodies (S1). In practice it is a turnkey project integrator. It bids for a government tender, supplies a mix of its own software modules, third-party OEM hardware and software, and subcontracted labour, then earns milestone payments and often a multi-year operations-and-maintenance tail (S1).

The work is organised into three verticals. Electronic governance covers traffic-enforcement systems, billing/revenue-cycle platforms, e-District, permit systems and cybersecurity. Telecommunications and broadband covers state-wide area networks, IP-MPLS, optical fibre roll-out and last-mile connectivity. Healthcare covers hospital information systems, RIS/PACS, revenue-cycle management and health-insurance platforms (S1). Its own product brands include RHES, AbHIS, Magnum PACS and RCM in healthcare; PlanPermit, AgniPermit, e-civic, e-District and InfoTrack in e-governance; and RConnect and RConverge in telecom (S1). The RHP notes that revenue from products and services is recognised on a bundled basis per order, so the product-versus-service split is not disclosed (S1).

blocks.caption: Revenue by vertical (Rs. million, restated consolidated) (S1)

blocks.text: The mix is moving toward e-governance project work and away from healthcare, the vertical where SRIT's own software IP (RHES, RCM) is most visible. Healthcare revenue nearly halved in FY26 and the healthcare order book is only Rs.424.24 mn (S1).

subsections.title: How revenue is earned: customers, projects and concentration

blocks.text: Government agencies and PSUs provided 89.41% of FY26 revenue (Rs.4,023.43 mn), against 91.34% in FY25 and 81.84% in FY24. Enterprises made up the rest (S1). Contracts are won through open tenders: SRIT pre-qualifies alone or in project-specific consortia and then submits a financial bid (S1). It bid on 43 tenders in FY26 and won 6, a 13.95% win ratio, with Rs.3,263.22 mn of awards. In FY25 it won 8 of 40 (Rs.881.52 mn), and in FY24 7 of 44 (Rs.9,666.57 mn) (S1). Named top-ten customers include RailTel Corporation of India, Telecommunications Consultants India (TCIL) and SEEPZ SEZ Authority. Other disclosed clients include ESIC, MP Textbook Corporation, CK Birla Hospital and Ebixcash (S1, S16).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration, share of revenue from operations (S1)

blocks.text:
Large marquee projects listed in the RHP are:
- A state-wide fibre network (about Rs.5,557.80 mn).
- Computerisation of a state-owned beverage distribution corporation (Rs.2,569.37 mn).
- 4G migration for about 15,000 ATMs of a public sector bank (Rs.2,508.19 mn).
- A Maharashtra forensic-lab integration, as consortium partner (Rs.3,028.37 mn).
- An AI traffic-enforcement system across 14 districts (Rs.1,512.27 mn).
- An ESIC health and ERP stack across about 2,200 hospitals and dispensaries (Rs.835.38 mn).
- A Qatar National Health Insurance System (about Rs.1,117.36 mn) (S1).
The company website identifies the fibre and traffic projects as KFON and Safe Kerala (S16). The RHP says Rs.136 mn of receivables older than three years relate mainly to BOOT-model projects, including Safe Kerala (S1).

items: Average active orders: 104 in FY26 (52 recurring, such as AMC/O&M, and 52 milestone-billed), against 120 in FY24 (S1)
Average revenue per client served rose from Rs.36.15 mn (FY24) to Rs.69.23 mn (FY26): fewer but larger clients (S1)
Revenue per average employee was Rs.3.90 mn in FY26. The employee base includes contractual staff and consultants, averaging 1,153 people (S1). Only 177 employees were permanent at 30 June 2026 (S4)

subsections.title: Operating model, supply chain and geography

blocks.text: There is no factory. The "capacity" is SRIT's ability to pre-qualify for tenders and then marshal subcontractors and OEM vendors. Revenue from projects executed through third-party subcontractors was Rs.2,656.10 mn (59.00%) in FY26, 66.18% in FY25 and 57.64% in FY24. Subcontracting and technical fees were Rs.3,216.68 mn, or 78.92% of total expenses, in FY26 (S1). The RHP states these subcontractors are unrelated to the promoters (S1). The main supplier-side risk is execution by these subcontractors. One subcontractor, Advantage SB Communications, failed on router supply for the ATM project and bought equipment from unauthorised OEMs. SRIT then extended an equipment loan of Rs.40.50 mn via Punjab & Sind Bank, which ASB defaulted on, and the matter is now in arbitration (S1).

State mix swings sharply from year to year as big projects start and finish. Maharashtra was 37.37% in FY25 but 10.12% in FY24, and Chhattisgarh was 19.79% in FY24 but 2.39% in FY26 (S1). This lumpiness is characteristic of tender-driven integrators. The international book is small and has shrunk from 13.93% of revenue in FY24 to 5.97% in FY26, led by a Qatar branch (S1).

Bottom line: SRIT is best understood as a government project integrator with some in-house software, not as a product or IP company. Its economics are governed by tender pricing, subcontractor costs and government payment cycles.

The RHP's industry chapter, from a Dun & Bradstreet report dated 27 August 2026 that the company commissioned and paid for, cites NASSCOM figures. India's domestic IT-BPM revenue was USD 51 bn in FY23 and USD 54 bn in FY24, and is estimated at USD 58.2 bn for FY25, growth of about 7% (S1). Government services, including e-governance, are estimated at about 7% of domestic IT-BPM revenue, healthcare about 7% and telecom about 5% (S1). That puts SRIT's addressable niches at a few billion dollars each in total. SRIT's own revenue of about USD 50 mn is a very small share.

Demand drivers cited are Digital India, BharatNet and state fibre networks, the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission and AI in public health, as well as state-level e-governance and smart-city spending (S1). India had about 944 mn broadband subscribers at March 2025, according to TRAI data quoted in the RHP (S1). These drivers are real, but they are policy-driven and budget-dependent. They are also available equally to every tender-qualified competitor.
The industry report was commissioned by the issuer for the IPO. It gives useful macro context but makes no independent market-share claim for SRIT in any segment.

For its own comparison, the RHP picks five listed peers: Mastek, RailTel Corporation of India, Protean eGov Technologies, Allied Digital Services and Aurionpro Solutions (S1). All are several times SRIT's size. Mastek's FY26 revenue from operations was Rs.36,987.50 mn, RailTel's Rs.42,774.80 mn, Aurionpro's Rs.14,110.85 mn, Protean's Rs.9,977.50 mn and Allied Digital's Rs.9,679.10 mn, against SRIT's Rs.4,499.99 mn (S1). The risk-factor section also names Practo, Napier Healthcare and MediBuddy in hospital IT, along with global vendors Cerner, Philips and Oracle Health (S1). In practice, government tenders also attract large IT services firms and many unlisted regional system integrators.

blocks.caption: Listed peers named in the RHP, FY26 revenue from operations (Rs. million) (S1)
rows: Telecom/broadband PSU. Also a top-10 SRIT customer and project partner

blocks.text: One notable point: RailTel is both a listed "peer" and one of SRIT's top-ten customers, and SRIT executes projects in collaboration with RailTel (S1). SRIT often sits one layer below a PSU prime contractor such as RailTel or TCIL. That position generally carries less pricing power than holding the government mandate directly.

The RHP's competitive-strength claims are:
- A 26-year track record.
- End-to-end integration capability.
- CMMI Level 5, SSE-CMM and ISO certifications.
- A diverse order book.
- An experienced promoter team (S1).
These are necessary to pre-qualify for large government tenders, and a long list of completed projects does raise the bar for new entrants on the biggest bids. But they are shared by every serious competitor. The RHP makes no import-substitution claim, no market-share claim, no sole-supplier claim, and cites no regulatory licence that keeps rivals out (S1).

The economics support that reading:
- Tenders are awarded largely on price once bidders qualify (S1).
- The win ratio is 14-20% (S1).
- EBITDA margins are 12.8-15.1% (S1).
- Nearly four-fifths of expenses are paid to subcontractors (S1).
In-house products such as RHES or RConverge exist, but the RHP itself describes RConverge as built on "legacy technology" that needs modernisation (S1). The client repeat rate of 73.85% shows some stickiness through O&M and AMC contracts (S1). That is incumbency, not a structural barrier.

Verdict on moat: none of substance. SRIT is a competent, experienced tender-qualified integrator in a crowded, price-driven market. Its advantages are credentials and relationships, not technology, scale or regulatory exclusivity.

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated key figures (Rs. million unless stated) (S1)

blocks.text: Growth has been strong but is slowing quickly: revenue growth went from 78.5% to 43.6% to 15.6% (S1). The FY25 margin dip is attributed in the MD&A to a turnkey project with heavy outsourcing and subcontracting (S1). FY26 margins recovered, but they remain in the thin band typical of integrators. Return ratios are falling as equity balloons from conversions and placements (S1). Note that FY24 tax expense was only Rs.12.62 mn on PBT of Rs.383.37 mn, against Rs.110.83 mn in FY25 (S1). FY24 PAT therefore benefited from an unusually low tax charge, which flatters the FY24 base and understates true PBT growth pressure.

Data caution: some aggregator pages show different figures. One broker page lists FY23-FY25 numbers that do not match the RHP, and another page describes the fresh issue as 1.68 lakh shares. This report uses only the RHP's restated numbers (S1, S12, S14).

blocks.caption: Balance sheet indicators (Rs. million) (S1, S4)
rows: Receivables + contract assets as % of total assets

blocks.text: Net worth doubled in FY26, but not only because of profits. The company raised Rs.285.01 mn through share issuance in pre-IPO placements at Rs.95 per share, and converted about Rs.280 mn of promoter loans into equity at Rs.70 per share (S1). Debt-to-equity looks low at 0.23. Even so, at 30 June 2026 fund-based borrowings were Rs.425.04 mn, including Rs.90.59 mn of loans from directors and Rs.106.46 mn of unsecured inter-corporate loans, plus Rs.560.56 mn of bank guarantees and surety bonds (S1). Contingent liabilities at FY26 add up to about Rs.634 mn (bank guarantees Rs.301.47 mn, surety bonds Rs.214.84 mn, plus tax and civil disputes) (S1, S6).

Working capital is the heart of the problem. Unbilled contract assets rose 59% in one year to Rs.1,538.01 mn. The RHP attributes this to percentage-of-completion revenue where milestone certification or invoicing is pending, on Kerala network projects, a Karnataka construction-workers welfare board project and TCIL-awarded projects (S1). Rs.136 mn of receivables are more than three years old (S1). The auditors also flagged that certain receivables and payables were classified as non-current in FY25, and that a Rs.568.35 mn provision was created for extinguishment of an inter-corporate deposit liability in the IGAAP accounts (S1).

subsections.title: Cash flow versus profit: does the trend support the story?

blocks.text: Cumulative PAT over FY24-FY26 was about Rs.1,060 mn, while cumulative operating cash flow was about Rs.400 mn (my calculation from S1). In FY26 the company reported record profit and burned cash. The FY26 gap was funded by share issuance (Rs.285.01 mn) and net new borrowing (S1). Cash and equivalents fell from Rs.241.44 mn to Rs.55.87 mn over two years (S1). The company has paid no dividends in FY24-FY26 or since (S1).

Profit growth is real on the P&L, but it has not converted to cash. Revenue growth has slowed to 15.6%, the order book is shrinking, and 57% of the IPO money is going simply to fund receivables. On those facts, the trend does not convincingly support a compounding-growth story.

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key terms (S1, S4, S9, S11)
rows: Book-built, 100% fresh issue, no offer for sale
Up to 16,800,000 equity shares of Rs.5 face value
QIB not more than 50%, NII not less than 15%, Retail not less than 35%
Opens 28 Sep 2026, closes 30 Sep 2026, allotment 1 Oct, listing 6 Oct 2026 (BSE, NSE)

blocks.text: Because there is no OFS, no existing shareholder is selling in the IPO, which is a genuine positive (S1, S10). Insiders have, however, already taken value out or come in cheaply before the IPO. In September 2024 the company bought back 6,712,400 shares (Rs.10 face value) at Rs.27 from the three promoters, a Rs.207.84 mn cash outflow (S1). In April 2025 promoter loans were converted into 4,003,353 shares at Rs.70 (Rs.5 face value) (S1). Between August and November 2025, 3,000,000 shares were placed with investors including Fortune Hands Growth Fund, NNM Securities and Valueaxis Wealth Advisors at Rs.95 (S1).
IPO buyers at Rs.130 pay 37% more than pre-IPO placees (Rs.95) and 86% more than the promoters' April 2025 loan conversion (Rs.70), barely a year earlier (my arithmetic from S1).

subsections.title: Objects of the issue, in full

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (Rs. million) (S1)
rows: Capex: modernisation and redevelopment of existing products
- RHES modernisation and 'OP LIVE' outpatient apps
Unidentified acquisitions, strategic initiatives and general corporate purposes
Balance (not quantified; capped at 35% of gross proceeds)

blocks.text: At the Rs.130 cap, the gross issue is Rs.2,184 mn. After the two quantified objects (Rs.1,368.57 mn), the balance of roughly Rs.815 mn less issue expenses goes to acquisitions, strategic initiatives and GCP. By SEBI rule that balance cannot exceed 35% of gross, or about Rs.764 mn, with each of acquisitions and GCP individually capped at 25% (my arithmetic from S1). The RHP says the company is in "preliminary and non-binding discussions" but has not identified any target. It lists smart metering, AI, analytics, e-education and health-tech as areas of interest, and undertakes that no acquisition will be from promoters, the promoter group or related parties (S1).

About 57% of the gross issue funds receivables, roughly 35% is discretionary with no named target, and under 6% goes to product modernisation. The objects have not been appraised by any bank or financial institution, and no orders have been placed for the capex. Vendor quotations only have been obtained (S1).

The three promoters are:
- Dr. Nambiar Raghavan Madhusoodan (67), MD and CEO, a director since incorporation, who holds 50.58% pre-issue. He previously worked at Baxter Fell Northfleet and International Agencies Co.
- His spouse Prasaktha Vakkiyl Nambiar (60), Whole-Time Director, with the company since 2003, working in training and HR.
- Martin Poovakkulam Chacko (59), Whole-Time Director since July 2019, a civil engineer previously with Services & Trade Company LLC, Indeset Trading and the SOBHA Group (S1).
The RHP discloses no other listed venture run by the promoters. It confirms that no director has been on the board of a suspended or delisted company (S1). Early shareholders included Services & Trade Company LLC and Sobha Limited (S1).

blocks.caption: Board composition (S1)
rows: Chairman, Independent (CA; ex-VST Tillers, Ballarpur Industries)
Non-Executive (co-founder, Carnot Research; retired Army colonel)

blocks.text: The entire independent board was assembled between April and December 2025, for the IPO. Two non-executive directors joined only on 10 August 2026, six weeks before the RHP (S1). The MD's pay package is a Rs.7.0 mn base salary with 10% annual step-ups, a Rs.3.5 mn allowance and a 2% commission on net profits, and it can be paid even in loss years under Schedule V (S1). He gave up the chairmanship on 10 August 2026 (S1).

blocks.caption: Material related-party transactions (Rs. million) (S1)
rows: Dr. Madhusoodan: loan converted to equity
P.V. Nambiar: loan converted to equity / buyback
M.P. Chacko: loans received / buyback / conversion
Liny Martin (relative of director): professional fees
Village Knowledge Development Centre (relative of director): manpower services
Ojus Health Care (controlled entity): rental income

blocks.text:
No promoter-linked supplier or customer sits in the revenue or cost base at any meaningful size. Payments to relatives' entities, such as manpower services and professional fees, are small, at a few million rupees a year (S1). That part is routine. The substance lies elsewhere, in a round-trip of capital between promoters and the company:
- In FY25 the promoters were paid Rs.181.24 mn in a buyback (107.08 + 37.91 + 36.25).
- In the same year they lent the company Rs.280.24 mn (186.08 + 47.91 + 46.25).
- That loan was converted to equity at Rs.70 in April 2025, 46% below the Rs.130 cap (S1).
Promoters were still owed Rs.89.10 mn in director loans and Rs.47.40 mn in unpaid remuneration at FY26-end (S1). Promoter directors also sit on the boards of subsidiary RICT India and the related entity Ojus Healthcare, and the independent chairman is also a director of RICT India (S1).

items: Auditor emphasis of matter, FY24: no provision was made for unspent CSR, relying on an expert opinion. FY24 and FY25: MSME supplier status not ascertained, so the required disclosures were not made (S1)
Two subsidiaries (SRIT Enterprise Solutions and SRIT Healthcare Solutions) were struck off in 2025 after being dormant, and the Rs.12.61 mn investment was written off (S1)

Tax: a service tax show-cause notice from 2013 with Rs.24.92 mn still disputed. GST demands for FY18-FY23 were Rs.33.23 mn at FY26. There are TDS default demands of Rs.8.38 mn, relating to late payment and filing defaults (S1)
Commercial disputes: the ASB subcontractor arbitration over the ATM project, and a Galmax Technologies arbitration claiming about Rs.25.16 mn on the Chhattisgarh e-District 2.0 project (S1)

Tender challenges: a writ petition in the Andhra Pradesh High Court over a cinema e-ticketing tender SRIT won is pending. A Kerala High Court PIL against the traffic-enforcement project was dismissed on 27 August 2025 (S1)

blocks.text: Nothing here amounts to fraud or regulatory enforcement against the promoters. But recurring tax and TDS lapses, unaddressed MSME and CSR compliance, a board assembled in the last 18 months, and cheap insider equity just before the IPO add up to below-average governance quality for a mainboard issuer.

items: Working capital and collection risk: receivables plus contract assets are 63.27% of total assets, operating cash flow was negative in FY26, and receivables older than three years total Rs.136 mn. Government payment delays tied to milestone certification are explicitly flagged (S1)
Government and tender dependence: 89.41% of revenue comes from government, won by competitive bidding at a 13.95% FY26 win ratio. A lean year of awards directly hits future revenue (S1)
Customer concentration: the top 3 are 57.93% and the top 10 89.36% of FY26 revenue, so losing or delaying one large project materially changes the numbers (S1)
Shrinking order book: down from Rs.14,769.56 mn (FY24) to Rs.11,828.24 mn (FY26). The RHP warns orders are subject to cancellation, modification and delay (S1)
Subcontractor dependence: subcontracting is 78.92% of expenses. SRIT is liable for subcontractor defaults, as in the ASB episode (S1)

blocks.text: These five risks reinforce each other. A tender integrator that subcontracts most delivery, bills on government milestones, and gets most of its revenue from a handful of state projects can show rising profits while cash lags. That is exactly the FY26 pattern (S1).
The single most decision-relevant risk is cash conversion. Record FY26 profit came with negative operating cash flow of Rs.121.01 mn, and 57% of the IPO is earmarked to fund working capital (S1).

items: Blank-cheque proceeds: up to 35% of gross proceeds goes to unidentified acquisitions and GCP, and the whole plan is unappraised (S1)
Execution risk on product modernisation: no definitive vendor agreements have been signed for the Rs.128.57 mn capex, and RConverge sits on a legacy stack (S1)
Promoter control: the MD alone holds 50.58% pre-issue and promoters keep 62.71% post-issue, with a profit-linked commission structure (S1, S4)
Litigation and contingent liabilities of about Rs.634 mn at FY26, including performance guarantees on TCIL and RVNL projects (S1, S6)
Foreign exchange: exposure in USD, QAR and EUR is unhedged, as the company uses no derivatives (S1)

blocks.text: The generic items in the RHP, such as macro, war, competition law and ASM/GSM surveillance, are excluded here because they apply to every issuer.

The capex object carries a specific inconsistency. Rs.92.84 mn of the Rs.128.57 mn goes to healthcare products (RHES/OP LIVE and RCM), even though healthcare revenue fell to Rs.330.51 mn in FY26 and the healthcare order book is just Rs.424.24 mn (S1). The spend may be justified by the Qatar NHIS reference, but it is a bet on reviving a shrinking vertical.

The RHP's strategy section sets out these plans (S1):
- Deploy AI across verticals. Examples include AI video analytics for a national highways authority toll project (Rs.79.00 mn) and an AI voice-chat citizen platform in Chhattisgarh (Rs.278.26 mn).
- Expand into the power-utility sector, starting from a Rs.597.56 mn transformer-monitoring project for a Karnataka power-generation corporation.
- Turn RConverge into an aggregator platform connecting ISPs and enterprises with last-mile service providers.
- Expand the healthcare and e-governance platforms geographically, including through the Qatar branch.
- Pursue acquisitions in smart metering, AI, analytics, e-education and health-tech.

At the IPO launch, management said the company had "built capabilities around designing, implementing and operating mission-critical digital platforms" and intends to strengthen its technology capabilities (S9). The RHP's MD&A describes the business as non-seasonal. It says there are no new business segments beyond those in the business section (S1).

No numeric revenue, margin or order-inflow guidance was found in the RHP or in press coverage reviewed. The outlook is qualitative. The one hard forward indicator is the order book of Rs.12,047.17 mn at 30 June 2026, and it has been falling (S1, S9).

The June 2026 order book is about 2.7 years of FY26 revenue (my calculation from S1), so there is reasonable visibility for FY27. Beyond that, growth depends on winning new large tenders. In FY26 SRIT won Rs.3,263.22 mn of new awards against Rs.4,499.99 mn billed (S1). Unless awards pick up, revenue growth is likely to keep decelerating from FY26's 15.6%. The strategic pivots (AI, power utilities, acquisitions) are early-stage: the power and AI projects cited are each well under 15% of annual revenue.

items: Positive signal to watch: FY27 order inflow above annual billing, and contract assets converting into receivables and then cash (S1)
Negative signal to watch: further growth in unbilled contract assets, or an acquisition announced soon after listing using the discretionary portion of proceeds (S1)

blocks.text: Management's stated plans are plausible, but none is quantified. Treat the growth story as unproven beyond the existing order book.

subsections.title: Anchor book, subscription and grey market

blocks.text: Before the issue opened, SRIT allotted 50,40,000 shares at Rs.130 to nine anchor investors, raising Rs.65.52 crore (S15, S5). The four largest allottees each took 15.26% of the anchor portion: Abakkus Venture Opportunities Fund 2, Founders Collective Fund, Taurus Mutual Fund (Taurus Ethical Fund) and Saint Capital Fund. Taurus is the only mutual fund in the book, with no large domestic AMCs, insurers or FPIs, as reported by IPO Central (S15). Half of the anchor shares are locked in for 30 days and half for 90 days from allotment (S5).

blocks.caption: Subscription status (S8, S5)
rows: 0x shown on trackers at time of writing

blocks.text: This report was written on the opening day. The trackers consulted showed no meaningful day-1 bid data yet, and Chittorgarh's subscription page said figures were not yet available (S5, S8). Nothing should be read into the day-1 figures in either direction. QIB and large NII bids typically arrive on the final day.

Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated): IPO Watch reported a GMP of Rs.32 on 26 Sep 2026, up from Rs.13 on 24 Sep (S7). IndiaIPO reported the same Rs.32 figure (S17). GMP is informal and easily moved, and it is not a basis for the investment call in this report.

method: Primary source: the SRIT India Red Herring Prospectus (S1). I downloaded it and read it page by page for the risk factors, capital structure, objects of the issue, business, industry overview, management, restated related-party note (Note 35), MD&A, cash flows, indebtedness and contingent liabilities. The RHP's own date could not be read off the cover, so 2026-09-22 is used as its date: that is the date of the auditor/KPI certificates cited inside it. I confirmed that the DRHP exists on SEBI (S2) and in the NSE archive (S3) but did not re-read the DRHP, since the RHP supersedes it with FY26 numbers. All financials come from the RHP's restated consolidated statements; figures in Rs. million are as printed. Derived ratios are my own arithmetic and are marked as such: receivable days, cumulative PAT versus operating cash flow, the residual for acquisitions/GCP, and order-book cover. Secondary sources (S4-S17) were used for issue terms, anchor allocation, shareholding post-issue, subscription status and GMP, and cross-checked against the RHP where possible. Several aggregator pages carry figures inconsistent with the RHP: Anand Rathi's FY23-FY25 table, Groww's '1.68 lakh shares' and H1 figures, and Upstox/Equity Research's DRHP-era CAGRs. These were not relied on. The anchor list and allocation percentages come from an IPO Central search-result summary, because the page itself returned HTTP 403; the total (50.4 lakh shares, Rs.65.52 cr) and the lock-in split were confirmed on Chittorgarh. Day-1 subscription figures were not meaningfully available at the time of writing. Material agreements with entities linked to the two August 2026 non-executive directors (Carnot Research, Blossom) were not reviewed in detail. Valuation (P/E, peer multiples) was deliberately excluded per the brief; peer names and revenues only are shown for competitive context.
